questions.prompt: Where does the AI Value Architect role sit in SAFe?

options.text: In the vendor and procurement function
On the Agile Release Train, helping it adopt AI
In the portfolio office, approving AI budgets
In a central data science group for the firm

questions.explanation: The framework describes AI Value Architects as dedicated roles on the train that help it adopt AI. Placing the role in a funding or central specialist group removes it from the day-to-day work it is meant to guide.

questions.prompt: How does SAFe describe the AI Value Architect's relationship to the business?

options.text: Accountable for the commercial result of each solution
Independent of business goals
Business-literate, without being the business owner
A delegate who signs off budgets

questions.explanation: The role is business-literate without being the Business Owners, AI-fluent without being the AI developers, and facilitative without being only a facilitator. Accountability for the commercial result stays with the business owners.

questions.prompt: A newly named AI Value Architect at Kessler Freight starts rewriting a team's prompts and model code herself. What does the role description suggest?

options.text: She should be AI-fluent while leaving the building to developers
She should report the team's mistakes to its line manager
She should stop engaging with the technical detail at all
She should take over the model work to protect its quality

questions.explanation: The role is AI-fluent without being the AI developer, so its job is to coach and connect. Taking over the work makes her a bottleneck and leaves the team no more capable than before.

questions.prompt: Which phrase sums up how the Value Architect course positions the role?

options.text: Facilitate, don't fix
Automate, then ask
Govern, don't engage
Build first, justify later

questions.explanation: The public course description presents the role as a connector and translator under the heading of facilitating and not fixing. Building first and justifying afterwards is the path to the proof of concept graveyard.

questions.prompt: Which of these is one of the five areas an AI Value Architect focuses on?

options.text: Coaching teams on responsible AI use
Approving each team's backlog
Writing the production model code
Selecting the enterprise model vendor

questions.explanation: The five areas are coaching on responsible use, finding better uses of existing tools, connecting business goals with technical execution, facilitating across roles while managing risk, and using data to measure success. Vendor selection and backlog approval are other people's decisions.

questions.prompt: Which existing roles does SAFe name as good candidates for the role?

options.text: Scrum Masters or Team Coaches, Product Managers and Architects
Newly hired data scientists alone
Finance controllers, auditors and procurement leads from the centre
External consultants on short contracts

questions.explanation: The public summary names Scrum Masters, Team Coaches, Product Managers and Architects as transition candidates, since they already connect people and work. People outside the train lack that standing with the teams.

questions.prompt: What does the term proof of concept graveyard describe?

options.text: A register of failed vendor contracts
Archived code from long-retired products
A backlog of rejected feature ideas
Promising demos that never reach scaled use

questions.explanation: The framework uses the phrase for AI initiatives that show promise as demonstrations and then never reach production at scale. It is about pilots that stall, not about products that had a full life.

questions.prompt: Which set of causes does SAFe give for AI initiatives stalling after the demo?

options.text: Leaders asked for too few pilots in the first year
Teams, sprints, demos and retrospectives were too frequent
Data, operations, risk, adoption and value were not prepared for
Models, tokens, vendors and hardware were too expensive

questions.explanation: The public text lists data not ready, operations not planned, risk not bounded, adoption not engineered and value not measured. Cost can matter, but the listed causes are about readiness around the model, not its price.

questions.prompt: A chatbot pilot at Lorimer Bank impressed executives, yet six months later nobody uses it. Staff were never trained and their workflow was unchanged. Which listed cause fits?

options.text: Risk was not bounded
Data was not ready for use
Adoption was not engineered
Value was not measured

questions.explanation: The tool worked but the way people work was never redesigned around it, which is the adoption gap. Data readiness is a common cause too, but nothing in the scenario points to a data problem.

questions.prompt: A pilot at Marchetti Health works on a curated sample but fails on live records with missing fields. Which listed cause fits?

options.text: Data was not ready
Operations were not planned
Adoption was not engineered
Value was not measured

questions.explanation: The gap between a clean sample and messy production data is the data readiness cause. Adoption could become a problem later, but the pilot has failed before any user is involved.

questions.prompt: An AI Value Architect supports a very small solution with one team. How do the responsibilities compare with those on a large solution?

options.text: They apply once the solution has scaled
They are the same; the size of the solution does not change them
They move to the team's product owner
They shrink to coaching, since small solutions carry little or no risk

questions.explanation: The framework states that the size of the solution does not change the responsibilities. A small solution can still fail on data, risk, adoption or value, so none of the five areas can be dropped.

questions.prompt: What does AI fluency mean for a Value Architect, according to the course description?

options.text: Memorising the parameters of each model
Writing production code in Python each day
Discussing technical trade-offs in business language
Training foundation models without engineers

questions.explanation: The course describes AI fluency as the ability to discuss trade-offs, such as the economics of retrieval versus fine-tuning, in business terms. It is fluency for translation, not engineering depth.

questions.prompt: A director at Nettleham Insurance asks whether to fine-tune a model or use retrieval for answers from policy documents that change weekly. Which reply shows AI fluency in business language?

options.text: Retrieval keeps answers current at lower cost; fine-tuning would need repeating each week
Both work, so choose whichever the vendor recommends
Wait until the models improve
Fine-tuning adjusts weights by gradient descent, while retrieval uses embeddings and an index

questions.explanation: The useful answer links the technical choice to cost and freshness, which is what the director is deciding on. The second option is accurate but gives the director nothing to decide with.

questions.prompt: A change agent at Ormsby Rail wants to build her own AI capability over the next quarter. Which plan is the strongest?

options.text: Pick one real task a week, apply AI to it, and note what worked
Read about each model release and wait for a formal course
Buy several tools and compare their features in a table
Ask the team to report what they learn each month

questions.explanation: Skill grows through regular, deliberate practice on real work with reflection. Reading about releases builds awareness but not the hands-on judgement others will rely on.

questions.prompt: Why does a personal AI roadmap matter for someone leading AI adoption?

options.text: Certification bodies require one before each renewal
It sets targets for other people's learning
It replaces the AI strategy of the whole organisation
Credibility with teams comes from visible, current practice

questions.explanation: People follow a change agent who demonstrably uses the tools and keeps learning. A personal roadmap is about the agent's own growth; it does not stand in for the organisation's strategy.

questions.prompt: An AI Value Architect at Pargeter Media has no line authority over the teams she supports. Which approach to influence fits best?

options.text: Ask the teams' managers to make her recommended tools mandatory for all staff
Show a working improvement on a team's own problem and let them judge it
Wait for teams to ask for help
Publish a policy and audit compliance

questions.explanation: Influence without authority rests on evidence, relevance and trust, and a result on the team's own pain is the most persuasive evidence. A mandate produces compliance without understanding and often quiet avoidance.

questions.prompt: Senior engineers at Quillfeather Bank are sceptical that AI helps with their legacy code. How should a change agent respond first?

options.text: Present industry statistics on the productivity gains reported elsewhere
Escalate their resistance to leadership
Ask what would convince them and run a small test on their code
Exclude them from the pilot

questions.explanation: Treating scepticism as a hypothesis to test respects their expertise and produces local evidence. Industry statistics rarely move people who believe their situation is different.

questions.prompt: Which stakeholder is most useful to engage early in an AI adoption effort?

options.text: An enthusiast with little standing among the delivery teams
A vendor representative
A manager who is leaving soon
A respected sceptic whose concerns expose real risks

questions.explanation: A respected sceptic brings the objections that would otherwise appear later, and their eventual support carries weight with peers. Enthusiasm without standing does not spread.

questions.prompt: Adoption of a coding assistant at Ravenscar Travel is flat. What should the change agent do before proposing a remedy?

options.text: Report the teams with the lowest usage figures
Replace the assistant with another vendor's product
Schedule more training sessions for each team
Diagnose the gap: skills, tooling, process or incentives

questions.explanation: Flat adoption has several possible causes, and the remedy for a skills gap differs from the remedy for a blocked workflow or a missing incentive. Training is the reflex answer and only fits one of them.

questions.prompt: Teams at Saxby Energy use the approved assistant, but security reviews reject its output and the work is redone by hand. Where is the gap?

options.text: In the process around the tool, not in individual skill
In the size of the licence pool
In the capability of the model
In the motivation of the developers who are using the assistant

questions.explanation: The tool is being used, but a downstream step cancels its benefit, so the surrounding process needs redesign with the security group. More motivation would not change the review outcome.

questions.prompt: Data scientists and product managers at Tiverton Health describe the same pilot in incompatible terms and blame each other for delay. What is the Value Architect's most useful contribution?

options.text: Document the dispute for leadership
Move the pilot to a single group
Decide which of the two groups is right and direct the other to comply
Translate between the groups and agree a shared definition of success

questions.explanation: The role is a connector and translator, so its contribution is a common language and a shared outcome. Ruling in favour of one side resolves the meeting but not the misunderstanding.

questions.prompt: Which activity is the clearest example of finding better ways to use existing AI tools?

options.text: Showing a team a feature of a licensed assistant that removes a manual step
Blocking tools that lack a business case
Negotiating a new enterprise contract with a second model provider this year
Building a custom model from scratch

questions.explanation: One of the five areas is finding better uses of tools the organisation already has. Buying more tools is a different activity and often leaves the existing ones underused.

questions.prompt: What does the course's Value Maximizer Playbook aim to unlock?

options.text: Budget for new AI platforms the organisation has not yet bought
Revenue from selling AI products
Headcount savings from automation
Unused potential in AI tools the organisation already owns

questions.explanation: The public description says the playbook uncovers and unlocks the large share of latent value in tools already owned. It starts from what is licensed today, not from new purchases.

questions.prompt: In which order does the Value Maximizer Playbook name its four steps?

options.text: Centralize, Audit, Activate, Optimize
Activate, Audit, Centralize, Optimize
Audit, Activate, Optimize, Centralize
Audit, Optimize, Activate, Centralize

questions.explanation: The certification page names the framework as Audit, Activate, Optimize, Centralize. It begins with finding out what exists and ends with bringing what works together.

questions.prompt: An organisation at Underhill Logistics does not know which AI features its existing licences include or who uses them. Which playbook step addresses this?

options.text: Activate
Optimize
Centralize
Audit

questions.explanation: By the plain meaning of the names, auditing is finding out what is owned and how it is used, which has to come before switching anything on. Activation without that picture is guesswork.

questions.prompt: A team at Vandermeer Pay has found a way of prompting that halves its review time. Under the playbook's last step, what should happen?

options.text: The practice is shared so other teams can reuse it
The practice is paused until it has been audited
The practice stays with the team as its advantage
The practice is replaced by a vendor template

questions.explanation: By its plain meaning, centralising brings proven practices into a shared place so value spreads beyond one team. Keeping it local leaves most of the organisation's potential unused.

questions.prompt: A team lead at Wetherby Rail asks the Value Architect to fix a failing prompt before a demo. What response develops the team?

options.text: Decline, since prompts are the team's job
Work through it with them so they can diagnose the next one
Rewrite the prompt for them and send it back before the demo starts
Suggest they cancel the demo

questions.explanation: Coaching through the problem leaves the team more capable, which is the point of the role. Fixing it for them solves today's demo and guarantees the same request next week.

questions.prompt: A Value Architect notices that every team brings its AI questions to her and none to each other. What does this indicate?

options.text: The questions should be routed to a helpdesk
She is succeeding, since the demand for her help continues to grow
She has become a bottleneck, and peers should share knowledge
The teams need more tools

questions.explanation: A change agent aims to make capability spread without passing through one person. Rising dependence looks like success but limits adoption to her own capacity.

questions.prompt: Developers at Yarborough Bank paste customer records into a public AI tool to save time. What should the Value Architect do first?

options.text: Ignore it for as long as the productivity results continue to look good
Ban AI tools across the train
Report the individuals to human resources
Coach them on responsible use and point them to an approved route

questions.explanation: Coaching teams on responsible AI use is one of the five areas, and an approved alternative lets the work continue safely. A ban removes the benefit and tends to push the practice out of sight.

questions.prompt: Leaders at Zeller Insurance ask the Value Architect to prove AI adoption by counting licences issued. What is the weakness of that measure?

options.text: It changes too often
It is hard to collect from the vendor
It reveals commercial terms
It counts access, not use or results

questions.explanation: A licence shows that someone could use a tool, not that they do or that work improved. Using data to measure success means choosing measures tied to outcomes.

questions.prompt: Which measure best shows that a change agent's coaching is working?

options.text: Teams give the sessions high ratings
Teams attend each of the coaching sessions they are offered
Teams request more licences
Teams apply AI to new tasks without asking for help

questions.explanation: Independent application to new problems shows capability has transferred. Attendance and satisfaction measure the coaching event, not its effect.

questions.prompt: A product manager wants an AI feature because a competitor has one. What question should a Value Architect ask first?

options.text: Which model and which vendor did the competitor choose for that feature?
Who will present it to executives?
Which customer or business outcome would it change, and by how much?
How soon can a demo be ready?

questions.explanation: Connecting business goals with technical execution starts from the outcome the work is meant to move. Copying a competitor's choice of model answers a question nobody has yet shown to matter.

questions.prompt: Two teams at Abbotsford Media use different AI tools for the same task and distrust each other's results. What enables collaboration best?

options.text: Separate backlogs so the teams do not overlap
A ruling from the architect on which of the two tools is to be the standard
A joint session comparing both on the same sample against agreed criteria
A freeze on both tools

questions.explanation: Shared evidence against criteria both teams accept replaces opinion with data and builds a working relationship. A ruling settles the tool question and leaves the distrust in place.

questions.prompt: Which topic does the exam list under Developing the AI-Native Change Agent?

options.text: Diagnosing gaps and enabling collaboration
Investment case and governance for each AI initiative
Iterative delivery and quick wins
Storytelling for impact

questions.explanation: The exam details page lists personal AI roadmap and skill-building, organisational influence and leadership, and diagnosing gaps and enabling collaboration for this domain. The other three topics belong to the strategy, value and delivery domains.

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the systems view this role brings?

options.text: An AI solution succeeds when the chosen model scores well on a widely used public benchmark
An AI solution succeeds through data, operations, risk, adoption and value together
An AI solution succeeds when the demo is approved
An AI solution succeeds when it is fully automated

questions.explanation: The framework says AI solution development needs a systems view linking strategy and technical execution. A strong model is one part; the stalled pilots it describes had working models.

questions.prompt: Match each quality in the role description to the boundary it is paired with.

options.text: Only a facilitator
The AI developer
The budget approver
The business owner

questions.explanation: The public role text pairs each quality with a boundary: literate in business without owning it, fluent in AI without building it, and facilitative without being limited to facilitation. Budget approval is not part of the description.

questions.prompt: An AI initiative at Brackley Bank involves legal, security, operations and two product lines. What should the Value Architect produce first?

options.text: A detailed delivery plan with dates for each of the teams involved
A demo for the executive sponsor
A map of stakeholders with their interests and influence
A vendor comparison

questions.explanation: Alignment starts with knowing who is affected, what each wants and how much say each has. A delivery plan written before that tends to be redrawn when an overlooked group objects.

questions.prompt: Legal at Carrow Health wants every AI output reviewed by a person; product wants full automation. Which approach resolves the conflict best?

options.text: Split the difference at half of outputs
Let the more senior of the two leaders decide the matter, and then move on
Explore the interests behind each position and vary the checks by risk
Postpone the feature until they agree

questions.explanation: The positions conflict, but the interests, safety and speed, can both be served by reviewing high-risk outputs and automating low-risk ones. Splitting at half serves neither interest well.

questions.prompt: Why is a conflict about an AI initiative better surfaced early than avoided?

options.text: Early conflict shows which teams to restructure
Unspoken objections return later as blocked releases
Avoided conflict costs the initiative nothing
Conflict is a sign the initiative should stop

questions.explanation: A concern that is not heard in design tends to reappear as a veto at approval or deployment, when change is expensive. Conflict is information about risk, not a verdict on the initiative.

questions.prompt: A sponsor at Dunmow Retail describes the goal as 'use AI in customer service'. What should the Value Architect do with that mandate?

options.text: Wait for a clearer instruction
Turn it into a specific outcome with a measure and an owner
Ask each team to propose a tool
Begin a pilot of the most popular chatbot product on the market

questions.explanation: A vague mandate cannot be aligned on or evaluated, so the first step is a concrete outcome such as shorter resolution time. Starting with a product commits to a solution before the problem is agreed.

questions.prompt: Operations at Elkstone Energy were not consulted on an AI scheduling tool and now refuse to support it. What would have prevented this?

options.text: Asking leadership to instruct the operations group
Choosing a tool that needs no support at all
Sending operations a briefing pack before launch
Involving operations when the solution was being shaped

questions.explanation: People support what they helped to shape, and operations would have raised its concerns while they were cheap to address. A briefing before launch informs people of a decision; it does not align them.

questions.prompt: Two business owners want the same data science capacity for different AI ideas. Which basis for deciding is strongest?

options.text: The order in which the two requests reached the team
The expected value and cost of delay of each idea
The seniority of each owner
An equal split of capacity

questions.explanation: Economic comparison gives a decision both owners can understand and accept. Splitting capacity evenly usually means both ideas arrive late.

questions.prompt: A steering group at Fairholme Pay cannot agree whether a pilot succeeded. What was missing at the start?

options.text: Success criteria agreed before the pilot began
A larger group of users enrolled from the first day
A more capable model
A longer pilot period

questions.explanation: Without criteria set in advance, each stakeholder judges the result against a private expectation. More users or more time would add data without settling what counts as success.

questions.prompt: A twelve-month plan for an AI programme at Glenmore Rail fixes scope, model and vendor in month one. What is the main weakness?

options.text: It lacks a named project manager
It commits before learning, in a field that changes within months
It should have been eighteen months
It gives the delivery teams too few milestones to report against each month

questions.explanation: Adaptive planning sets a direction and near-term commitments, then adjusts as evidence arrives. Locking model and vendor for a year ignores how quickly capability and prices move.

questions.prompt: Which planning approach suits an AI initiative with uncertain feasibility?

options.text: Short cycles, each ending in a decision to continue, change or stop
A fixed scope with flexible quality
A single business case, approved once and then delivered to its plan
A plan revised at the end of the programme

questions.explanation: Short cycles limit the amount at risk before the next piece of evidence. A single up-front approval assumes the answers are already known.

questions.prompt: A pilot at Hartwell Insurance shows accuracy below the agreed threshold after two cycles. Which response reflects adaptive planning?

options.text: Review the evidence and decide to pivot, narrow the scope or stop
Continue as planned, since the budget for the year is already approved
Hide the result until accuracy improves
Lower the threshold so the pilot passes

questions.explanation: The point of a threshold is to trigger a decision when it is missed. Moving it to fit the result removes the control and sends an unsafe solution forward.

questions.prompt: What are the course's Feasibility Filters for?

options.text: Filtering model output for unsafe content
De-risking an initiative before code is written
Ranking candidate vendors by their price
Selecting who attends a design workshop

questions.explanation: The certification page describes Feasibility Filters as a way to de-risk an initiative before any code is written. The name can suggest content filtering, which is a runtime safety control and a different thing.

questions.prompt: A team at Ingleby Media wants to start building an AI summariser this week. When should feasibility be tested?

options.text: During the final security review
After the first release, once the usage data becomes available to it
Before any code, while a change of direction is still cheap
At the next annual planning cycle

questions.explanation: The idea of filtering for feasibility is to find the blocking problem before money is spent on code. Usage data after release is valuable, but it arrives too late to prevent an avoidable failure.

questions.prompt: Which question bounds the risk of an AI initiative most directly?

options.text: What is the worst outcome of a wrong answer, and who catches it?
Which team will present the demo?
How many users will the pilot have?
Which of the available models has the highest benchmark score today?

questions.explanation: Risk is bounded by knowing the harm a failure can cause and the control that limits it. The framework lists risk not bounded among the reasons pilots stall.

questions.prompt: An AI assistant drafts replies to customers at Jesmond Bank. Which control fits a case where a wrong reply could cause financial harm?

options.text: Replies are sampled for review once a quarter
A person reviews each reply before it is sent
The model is asked to check itself
A disclaimer is added below each reply

questions.explanation: Where a wrong output can cause real harm, a human approval step before the output takes effect is the proportionate control. A disclaimer shifts blame without preventing the harm.

questions.prompt: The same assistant also suggests internal article tags, where mistakes are harmless and easy to correct. Which level of oversight is proportionate?

options.text: No monitoring at all
Review by the legal team
Approval of each tag by two reviewers before it is published
Automatic use with monitoring and periodic sampling

questions.explanation: Oversight should match the consequence of error; low-risk, reversible outputs can flow with monitoring. Double approval for tags spends scarce attention where it prevents nothing.

questions.prompt: A team at Kirkby Pay plans to send customer transaction data to an external model API. What must be settled first?

options.text: Whether the data's classification and contract terms permit it
Whether the API's response time is fast enough for the feature
Whether the team has enough licences
Whether the prompt is short enough

questions.explanation: Data protection obligations decide whether the design is allowed at all, so they come before performance. A fast answer built on a prohibited data flow has to be thrown away.

questions.prompt: A retrieval assistant at Lanchester Health can read any document on the shared drive. Which risk is most direct?

options.text: Users may see content they are not authorised to see
The model may need retraining
The index may grow large
Users may find that their answers arrive a little more slowly

questions.explanation: If retrieval ignores document permissions, the assistant becomes a way around access control. Retrieval should enforce the same permissions as the source system.

questions.prompt: An agent at Maddox Logistics can read emails and also issue refunds. Which design principle limits the damage of a manipulated instruction?

options.text: A longer system prompt that tells the agent to behave honestly
A more capable model
A faster rollback of the model version
Least privilege, with approval for irreversible actions

questions.explanation: Limiting what the agent may do and requiring approval before irreversible actions contains the effect of a prompt injection. Instructions in a prompt are advice the model can be talked out of.

questions.prompt: Which risk is specific to generative AI and absent from conventional software?

options.text: Downtime of a hosting provider
Plausible output that is factually wrong
Licences that expire
Defects introduced by a change to the code

questions.explanation: Generative models can produce fluent, confident and false statements, so their output needs grounding or verification. The other risks apply to any software system.

questions.prompt: Which cost is most often missed in the investment case for an AI solution?

options.text: The licence fee for the model during the first month of the pilot
The cost of the demo
The salary of the sponsor
Ongoing evaluation, monitoring and maintenance after launch

questions.explanation: Running an AI solution includes monitoring quality, handling drift, updating prompts and data, and human review, which often exceed the build cost over time. The pilot licence is small and visible.

questions.prompt: A pilot at Norham Retail costs little per day with fifty users. What must the investment case examine before scaling to fifty thousand?

options.text: Which colour scheme the interface uses
How usage-based cost grows with volume
Whether the pilot users enjoyed taking part
How many slides the case has

questions.explanation: Model usage is typically priced per unit of text processed, so cost scales with users and requests. A pilot that is cheap at fifty users can be uneconomic at scale.

questions.prompt: From a cost point of view, when is fine-tuning easier to justify than retrieval?

options.text: When answers must cite their sources
When a stable, specialised behaviour is needed at high volume
When the source documents are revised by their owners each week
When the budget for data preparation is zero

questions.explanation: Fine-tuning has an up-front cost that pays back when the behaviour is stable and used heavily. Frequently changing documents favour retrieval, because the knowledge can be updated without retraining.

questions.prompt: Which statement belongs in a sound investment case for an AI initiative?

options.text: A list of the features of the chosen model
A baseline, the expected change, and how it will be measured
A promise that the solution pays back within a quarter
A comparison with a competitor's press release

questions.explanation: A case that names the current baseline and the measurable change can be checked later. A promised payback without a baseline cannot be verified.

questions.prompt: Leaders at Oxenhope Energy want to fund ten AI pilots at once. What is the stronger investment approach?

options.text: Fund the cheapest ten ideas
Hold all funding until one vendor is chosen
Fund all ten in full, so that each one of them can keep to its schedule
Fund a few in small increments and release more as evidence arrives

questions.explanation: Incremental funding tied to evidence limits loss on ideas that fail and moves money to those that work. Full funding for ten pilots is how the proof of concept graveyard fills.

questions.prompt: An investment case lists 'hours saved' as its single gain. What is the weakness?

options.text: Saved hours are a benefit only if they turn into an outcome
Saved hours should be reported weekly
Saved hours apply to developers alone
Saved hours are too difficult for a finance team to count at all

questions.explanation: Time saved has value when it becomes shorter lead time, more output or lower cost. Otherwise it is a capacity estimate that never reaches the result leaders care about.

questions.prompt: Which governance arrangement supports both speed and safety for AI use?

options.text: A ban on external models
No rules until a problem occurs
A committee that approves each AI use case before any work starts
Clear guardrails that teams work within without asking each time

questions.explanation: Guardrails set the limits once and let teams decide inside them, which keeps flow and control together. Approval of every case creates a queue and encourages people to work around it.

questions.prompt: A team asks whether it may use a new AI tool. Which answer reflects good governance?

options.text: Use it quietly until someone elsewhere in the organisation objects to it
Check it against the published criteria for data, security and use
Wait for the annual policy review
Ask the vendor whether it is safe

questions.explanation: Published criteria let teams get a fast, consistent answer. Quiet use without a check is how unapproved tools spread and data leaves the organisation.

questions.prompt: Who stays accountable for a decision that an AI system recommended?

options.text: The team that wrote the prompt
The person or role that acted on it
The AI system itself
The vendor that supplied the model

questions.explanation: Accountability stays with people; AI output is an input to a human decision. Vendors carry contractual duties, but they do not own the organisation's decisions.

questions.prompt: Which four functions form the core of the NIST AI RMF?

options.text: Govern, Map, Measure, Manage
Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond
Audit, Activate, Optimize, Centralize
Plan, Do, Check, Act

questions.explanation: The NIST AI RMF is organised around Govern, Map, Measure and Manage. Identify, protect, detect and respond come from NIST's cybersecurity framework, which is the tempting confusion.

questions.prompt: What is the status of the NIST AI Risk Management Framework?

options.text: It is intended for voluntary use
It applies to government agencies alone
It is a certification scheme
It is a binding federal regulation

questions.explanation: NIST describes the framework as intended for voluntary use to help manage AI risks and build trustworthiness. It is guidance, unlike the EU AI Act, which is law.

questions.prompt: How does the EU AI Act classify AI systems?

options.text: By level of risk
By the country of the provider
By the type of model architecture
By the size of the provider company

questions.explanation: The Act takes a risk-based approach with four levels: unacceptable, high, transparency and minimal risk. Obligations follow the risk of the use, not the technology or the size of the company.

questions.prompt: Which four risk levels does the European Commission describe for the AI Act?

options.text: Red, amber, green and blue
Critical, major, moderate and minor risk for each of the systems
Unacceptable, high, transparency, and minimal or no risk
Banned, licensed, registered and exempt

questions.explanation: The Commission describes unacceptable risk, high risk, transparency risk, and minimal or no risk. The other sets resemble common risk scales but are not the Act's categories.

questions.prompt: A recruiter at Penhallow Group plans to use AI to sort job applications. Which AI Act risk level does the Commission give as the example for this?

options.text: Transparency risk
High risk
Minimal risk
Unacceptable risk

questions.explanation: CV-sorting software for recruitment is one of the Commission's examples of a high-risk use. It is permitted, but it carries duties such as risk management, data quality, documentation and human oversight.

questions.prompt: A retailer at Quinton Stores deploys a customer chatbot. What does the AI Act's transparency duty require?

options.text: Users receive the training data on request
Users are shown the system prompt in each chat
Users must consent in writing before each chat
Users are told they are interacting with a machine

questions.explanation: The transparency obligations require that people know they are talking to an AI system, and that AI-generated content such as deepfakes is identifiable. They do not require disclosure of training data to each user.

questions.prompt: Which practice is prohibited under the AI Act?

options.text: Chatbots that disclose they are AI
Spam filtering of incoming mail
Social scoring
Credit scoring with human oversight

questions.explanation: Social scoring is among the prohibited practices classed as unacceptable risk. Credit scoring is a high-risk use that is allowed with safeguards, and spam filters are the Commission's example of minimal risk.

questions.prompt: An employer at Rushmere Works wants AI that infers employees' emotions during meetings to rate their engagement. How does the AI Act treat emotion recognition in the workplace?

options.text: It is a high-risk use with safeguards
It needs a transparency notice alone
It is a prohibited practice
It is a minimal-risk use

questions.explanation: Emotion recognition in workplaces and schools is on the list of prohibited practices. It is easy to assume it is high risk and manageable, but the Act bans it.

questions.prompt: From which date do the AI Act's rules for stand-alone high-risk use cases apply, according to the Commission page checked on 14 Nov 2026?

options.text: 2 February 2025
2 December 2027
2 August 2026
2 August 2028

questions.explanation: The Commission page gives 2 December 2027 for the listed high-risk use cases such as employment and education. The August 2028 date is for high-risk AI embedded in regulated products.

questions.prompt: From which date do the rules for high-risk AI embedded in regulated products apply?

options.text: 2 December 2027
2 August 2028
2 August 2025
2 August 2026

questions.explanation: High-risk AI that is a component of products such as lifts or toys follows from 2 August 2028. The December 2027 date is for the stand-alone use cases.

questions.prompt: It is November 2026. Which AI Act obligations already apply to a company in the EU that deploys a public chatbot?

options.text: The bans, AI literacy duties and transparency rules
The product safety rules for embedded AI
The high-risk duties for the listed use cases
None, since the Act applies from 2028

questions.explanation: Prohibitions and AI literacy applied from February 2025 and transparency rules from August 2026. The duties for listed high-risk uses start in December 2027, so they are not yet in force. Duties for general-purpose models also apply already, but they fall on model providers.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a duty of a provider of a high-risk AI system?

options.text: Annual renaming of the system
Publication of the model weights for inspection by the public
Human oversight, logging and detailed documentation
Free access for all users

questions.explanation: The Commission lists risk assessment and mitigation, high-quality datasets, activity logging, documentation, information for deployers, human oversight, and robustness and accuracy. Open publication of weights is not among them.

questions.prompt: A governance lead says 'we follow the NIST framework, so we comply with the EU AI Act'. What is wrong with that?

options.text: The NIST framework has replaced the Act
The Act applies to model providers alone
Both are optional documents, so neither of them creates a duty to comply
One is voluntary guidance; the other is law with its own duties

questions.explanation: The NIST AI RMF is voluntary guidance, while the AI Act sets legal obligations by risk level and applies to deployers as well as providers. Following one can help with the other, but it does not establish compliance.

questions.prompt: Which topic does the exam list under Strategy, Alignment, and Governance?

options.text: Measuring value
Adaptive planning and risk management
Personal AI roadmap and skill-building
Readiness and momentum

questions.explanation: The exam details page lists stakeholder alignment and conflict management, adaptive planning and risk management, and investment case and governance for this domain. It is the largest domain, at 33 to 37 percent.

questions.prompt: Match each example to its AI Act risk level, as the European Commission gives them.

options.text: Systemic risk
Unacceptable risk
Transparency risk
Minimal or no risk
High risk

questions.explanation: These are the Commission's own examples for the four levels. Systemic risk is a term used for some general-purpose models and is not one of the four levels for AI systems.

questions.prompt: In which order does the course name the phases of the AI-Native solution lifecycle?

options.text: Discover, Sense, Deliver, Design
Design, Discover, Deliver, Sense
Sense, Discover, Design, Deliver
Sense, Design, Discover, Deliver

questions.explanation: The certification page names the phases as Sense, Discover, Design and Deliver. Design follows Discover, because a solution is shaped after the problem and its constraints are understood.

questions.prompt: What do the Sense, Discover, Design and Deliver phases turn a vague mandate into?

options.text: A signed contract with a model provider for the new solution
A production deployment in one step
A finalized, cross-functional AI-Native Value Blueprint
A portfolio epic with full funding

questions.explanation: The public description says the phases turn a vague mandate into a finalized, cross-functional AI-Native Value Blueprint. The blueprint is an agreed design across functions, not a contract or a deployment.

questions.prompt: Why does the blueprint need to be cross-functional?

options.text: The technology team lacks authority
Each function needs its own separate copy of the project plan to sign
More signatures make the approval safer
Data, operations, risk and adoption sit in different functions

questions.explanation: The causes of stalled pilots lie across data, operations, risk, adoption and value, and no single function controls them all. A blueprint agreed by one function leaves the others to object later.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of planning the full solution lifecycle before a demo is celebrated?

options.text: To give the vendor a longer contract
To delay the demo until all is specified
To get from demonstration to production use
To take the place of iterative delivery

questions.explanation: The course describes a blueprint for the whole lifecycle, from demo to production, as the way out of the proof of concept graveyard. Planning the path does not mean specifying everything before starting.

questions.prompt: A team at Sedgwick Bank must choose a first AI use case. Which one makes the best quick win?

options.text: A task nobody currently measures
A frequent, low-risk task with a visible and measurable result
A high-profile, high-risk decision that leaders care a great deal about
A task that happens once a year

questions.explanation: A quick win is small, safe and visibly useful, so it builds confidence and evidence. A high-risk decision as a first case invites a public failure before the organisation has learned anything.

questions.prompt: Why do quick wins matter beyond their direct benefit?

options.text: They end the need for a written business case
They let the organisation skip later governance
They prove the largest use case will work
They create evidence and momentum for the larger change

questions.explanation: Early, credible results give sponsors a reason to continue and sceptics a reason to engage. They do not prove that harder use cases will succeed, and governance still applies.

questions.prompt: An AI drafting tool at Tolworth Media is built in one large release after nine months, and users reject it. What would iterative delivery have changed?

options.text: The budget would have been approved sooner
The release would have been larger and later still
Users would have shaped it through early, small releases
Users would have received a longer manual at release

questions.explanation: Delivering in small increments puts working output in front of users early, when their feedback can still change the design. A single late release tests every assumption at once.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the best first increment for an AI assistant that answers policy questions?

options.text: The full knowledge base for all staff at once, released without any citations
A model fine-tuned on every document
An architecture document for review
Answers for one topic area, with sources, for a small group of users

questions.explanation: A thin slice that works end to end for a narrow scope gives real feedback at low risk. Covering everything at once hides which part fails.

questions.prompt: Before delivery starts at Upwell Health, the Value Architect checks whether records are complete, accessible and permitted for use. Which kind of readiness is this?

options.text: Data readiness
Operational readiness
Adoption readiness
Financial readiness

questions.explanation: Data not being ready is the first cause the framework lists for stalled initiatives. Operational readiness is a separate check, about who runs and supports the solution.

questions.prompt: Nobody at Varley Pay has decided who will monitor an AI solution's quality after launch or respond when it degrades. Which readiness gap is this?

options.text: Operations were not planned
Value was not measured
Data was not ready for use
Risk was not bounded

questions.explanation: Running an AI solution needs monitoring, ownership and a response path, which is the operations cause in the framework's list. The gap here is about who runs it, not about the data it uses.

questions.prompt: A readiness check finds that data is ready but frontline staff have not been involved. What is the sensible decision?

options.text: Proceed with a small scope and bring staff into the design
Stop the initiative
Replace the staff concerned
Proceed at full scale, since the technical risk has been retired

questions.explanation: Readiness is uneven in practice, so the response is to limit scope and close the gap, not to ignore it or abandon the work. Technical readiness without adoption readiness is how working tools go unused.

questions.prompt: Enthusiasm for an AI programme at Wickham Rail fades three months after a good start. What sustains momentum best?

options.text: A regular cadence of visible results and shared learning
A stricter usage policy
A single annual showcase event held for the executive team
A new logo for the programme

questions.explanation: Momentum comes from frequent, concrete evidence that the change is working, shared widely. An annual event is too rare to keep attention.

questions.prompt: The Value Architect facilitates a design workshop. Who needs to be in the room?

options.text: The sponsor and the vendor
The facilitator and one note-taker
Business, technology, data, risk and the people who will use the solution
The architects and the data scientists, with all the others briefed afterwards

questions.explanation: Design decisions touch value, feasibility, data, risk and daily work, so each perspective has to be present when trade-offs are made. Briefing people afterwards gets their objections after the design is fixed.

questions.prompt: During a design workshop, a senior architect asks the Value Architect to choose the model. What is the facilitative response?

options.text: Defer the decision to the vendor
End the session and decide later alone
Choose the model with the best reputation, to keep things moving
Frame the options and trade-offs so the group can decide

questions.explanation: The role facilitates and does not fix, so its contribution is to make the choice and its consequences clear to the people who own it. Choosing for the group makes the facilitator the owner of a decision they will not live with.

questions.prompt: A design session at Yaxley Energy produces a long list of ideas and nothing chosen. What should the facilitator have set up?

options.text: A vote on the facilitator
A longer session, with more ideas from each participant
A smaller room
Agreed criteria and a decision step in the agenda

questions.explanation: A design session needs both divergence and convergence, and criteria agreed in advance make the convergence possible. More time for ideas adds to the list without producing a choice.

questions.prompt: What belongs in the design of an AI solution besides the model and the prompt?

options.text: The vendor's marketing material
The source code of the model
The changed workflow, the human checkpoints and the measures of success
The office seating plan for the teams and the calendar of their social events

questions.explanation: An AI solution is a redesigned piece of work, so its design covers who does what, where people review output and how success is measured. A design that stops at the model produces a demo.

questions.prompt: A team wants to automate a claims process end to end in its first release. What does iterative delivery suggest?

options.text: Run the old and the new processes together for a year
Wait for a model that needs no human oversight at all
Assist people on one step first, then extend as evidence allows
Automate the whole process at once for the full benefit

questions.explanation: Starting with assistance on one step limits risk and shows where the solution is reliable enough to extend. Full automation in one release bets everything on untested assumptions.

questions.prompt: Which topic does the exam list under the solution and delivery domain?

options.text: Stakeholder alignment and conflict management
Facilitating the Design phase
Organizational influence and leadership
Communicating results

questions.explanation: The exam details page lists iterative delivery and quick wins, readiness and momentum, and facilitating the Design phase for this domain. It is the smallest domain, at 15 to 16 percent.

questions.prompt: Put the phases of the AI-Native solution lifecycle in order.

options.text: Sense
Deliver
Design
Discover

questions.explanation: The course names the phases in this order. Sense comes first and Deliver last, with discovery of the problem before design of the solution.

questions.prompt: What does the course's AI-Powered Story Amplifier do?

options.text: Generates marketing copy for the products and the services of the organisation
Turns technical success metrics into a narrative for senior leaders
Summarises team retrospectives
Increases the volume of model output

questions.explanation: The certification page describes it as turning technical success metrics into a C-suite-ready narrative. Its purpose is internal: to secure funding and adoption, not to market products.

questions.prompt: Which two things is the story meant to secure, according to the course description?

options.text: Patents and licences
Certification and audits
Funding and adoption
Headcount and office space

questions.explanation: The public description says the narrative is used to secure funding and adoption. A result that leaders cannot understand rarely receives either.

questions.prompt: A team reports to executives that its model reached '0.91 F1 on the validation set'. How should the Value Architect reframe this?

options.text: State what changed for customers or costs because of that accuracy
Show the confusion matrix
Explain how the F1 score is calculated
Add the precision and the recall figures alongside the F1 score on the slide

questions.explanation: Executives decide on outcomes, so the message should say, for example, that nine in ten claims are now routed correctly without manual triage. More technical detail answers a question they did not ask.

questions.prompt: Which structure has the most impact with a senior audience?

options.text: The technology, the architecture, the roadmap, and then finally the benefit
The team members, the tools, and the timeline
A list of all metrics collected
The problem, what was done, the measured result, and the next decision

questions.explanation: A story that opens with the problem the audience recognises and ends with a decision they can make is the one that moves them. Leading with technology loses them before the benefit appears.

questions.prompt: Why should a results story include a specific person or team affected by the change?

options.text: Named individuals can then be held responsible for the outcome
Concrete examples make the numbers credible and memorable
It removes the need for data
It makes the presentation longer

questions.explanation: A single case that the audience can picture gives meaning to the aggregate figures. The example supports the data; it does not replace it.

questions.prompt: The same pilot result must be presented to engineers and to the finance director. What should change?

options.text: Nothing; one deck suits both
The figures, so that each audience hears what it prefers to hear
The emphasis and language, while the facts stay the same
The conclusion

questions.explanation: Each audience cares about different consequences of the same facts, so the framing adapts. Changing the figures by audience destroys trust the first time the two compare notes.

questions.prompt: Which measure best shows the value of an AI assistant for support agents?

options.text: Change in resolution time and customer satisfaction against a baseline
Number of prompts sent to the assistant by the agents on each day of the week
Number of agents with a licence
Number of features in the assistant

questions.explanation: Value shows in the outcome the assistant was meant to improve, compared with what it was before. Prompt counts measure activity and can rise while outcomes stay flat.

questions.prompt: What is a baseline when judging value?

options.text: The first version of the model
The target that the sponsor hopes to reach
The minimum budget for the pilot
The measured state before the change

questions.explanation: A baseline is the level of the measure before the change, against which improvement is judged. Without it, a result cannot be attributed to the initiative.

questions.prompt: A pilot at Aldgate Insurance reports faster claims handling, but no measurement was taken beforehand. What can be concluded?

options.text: The pilot failed
Little, since there is nothing to compare the result with
The pilot succeeded, because the handlers say it feels much faster
The model is accurate

questions.explanation: Without a baseline, the improvement is an impression. This is the value not measured cause that leaves pilots unable to justify scaling.

questions.prompt: Which pair gives a balanced view of an AI solution's value?

options.text: Two satisfaction surveys of the project team
An early usage signal and a later business outcome
Two usage counts from the same dashboard
Two financial results taken a year apart

questions.explanation: A leading indicator shows early whether the change is taking hold, and a lagging outcome confirms the business effect. Two measures of the same kind leave half the picture missing.

questions.prompt: Usage of an AI tool at Bramhall Bank is high, but the outcome it was meant to improve has not moved. What is the right conclusion?

options.text: The outcome measure should be dropped
The initiative has succeeded, since high usage was the agreed goal
The tool needs more users
Adoption is not the same as value; examine how the tool is used

questions.explanation: High usage with no outcome change suggests the tool is used for low-value tasks or its output is discarded downstream. Declaring success on usage alone confuses activity with benefit.

questions.prompt: An AI feature raises output per developer, but defects in production rise too. How should the effect be reported?

options.text: Report the defects to the team alone
Report both, since value includes quality as well as speed
Report neither until both improve
Report the output gain and investigate the defects separately later

questions.explanation: A measure of speed without its quality counterpart overstates the benefit. Leaders making a funding decision need the whole effect.

questions.prompt: A pilot at Colby Retail missed its target. What is the right way to communicate that?

options.text: Attribute the result to the work of the data team
Present the secondary metrics that happened to improve
State the result, what was learned, and the recommended decision
Delay the report until a better result is available

questions.explanation: Honest reporting with a recommendation keeps trust and lets leaders redirect money promptly. Switching to whichever metric improved is a habit that makes later good news unbelievable.

questions.prompt: Why is a negative pilot result still valuable to the organisation?

options.text: It stops further spending on an idea the evidence does not support
It proves AI does not work here
It reduces the need for governance
It shows which of the teams should be removed from the later pilots

questions.explanation: An early, cheap 'no' is one of the main returns on a small experiment. It says something about one hypothesis, not about AI in general or the people involved.

questions.prompt: How often should results from an AI initiative be shared with stakeholders?

options.text: After each model upgrade
When a stakeholder asks
On a regular cadence, including when there is little to show
Once, when the final outcome has been confirmed by the finance team

questions.explanation: Regular updates keep stakeholders aligned and make surprises small. Waiting for a final outcome leaves a long silence in which support drifts.

questions.prompt: Staff at Dunstan Health fear an AI scheduling tool will be used to cut jobs. What should the communication include?

options.text: What will change in their work, what will not, and how they can shape it
The productivity targets that the new tool is expected to help the hospital achieve
A reminder that use is mandatory
Technical details of the model

questions.explanation: People adopt a change when they understand its effect on them and have a say in it. Leading with productivity targets confirms the fear the message needed to address.

questions.prompt: A tool is deployed and trained on, yet people return to the old way within a month. What does organisational change require beyond rollout?

options.text: Removal of the old tool's documentation
A second training session that repeats the first session's content in full
A stronger mandate
Reinforcement: updated processes, measures and leadership behaviour

questions.explanation: A change holds when the surrounding system supports it: the process expects the new way, measures reflect it and leaders model it. Repeating the training treats a system problem as a knowledge gap.

questions.prompt: Which sign shows that an AI practice has become part of how an organisation works?

options.text: The vendor contract was renewed
New work is designed with it by default, without a special programme
Every employee has completed the course
A dedicated programme office reports on its usage to leaders each month

questions.explanation: A change is embedded when it no longer needs separate attention to continue. A programme office reporting on usage shows the change is still being pushed from outside.

questions.prompt: A person in this role is asked what she contributes if she does not build models or own the budget. Which answer fits?

options.text: She uses data to show whether AI work is producing the intended value
She approves which teams may use AI
She guarantees that each one of the AI initiatives will be successful
She replaces the product manager

questions.explanation: Using data to measure success is one of the five areas of the role, with coaching, connecting and facilitating. No role can guarantee outcomes; this one makes them visible and improvable.

questions.prompt: Leaders ask for the return on an AI coding assistant after one month. What is the most honest reply?

options.text: Decline to report until the year ends
Give a precise annual return, extrapolated from the first month's usage data
Report the vendor's published figures
Share early indicators now and say when outcome data will be meaningful

questions.explanation: Early signals are useful if they are labelled as such, with a date for firmer evidence. A precise annual figure from one month looks rigorous and is a guess.

questions.prompt: Which topic does the exam list under Value Realization and Organizational Change?

options.text: Iterative delivery and quick wins
Investment case and the governance of AI initiatives
Diagnosing gaps and enabling collaboration
Storytelling for impact

questions.explanation: The exam details page lists storytelling for impact, measuring value and communicating results for this domain. The investment case belongs to the strategy domain.

questions.prompt: Match each measure to its kind.

options.text: Lagging outcome
Input, not a result
Baseline
Leading indicator
Guardrail

slots.text: Share of agents using the assistant each week
Resolution time last quarter, before the change

questions.explanation: Weekly usage signals early adoption, satisfaction after six months is an outcome, last quarter's figure is the baseline and licences are an input. A guardrail is a limit on behaviour and is not a kind of value measure.
